narrative:
The model predicts an 84% chance that you will leave your job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This high probability signals that, based on patterns from many similar employees, the company sees a strong risk of you departing soon.

Three key factors drove this outlook, ranked by their influence. First, having received other job opportunities while in your current role was the strongest push toward leaving. Most employees predicted to stay (77%) had not received such offers, but you did, which the model interprets as you having viable alternatives that increase turnover risk.

Second, your overall career experience of 6-10 years also nudged the prediction toward leaving. While this is fairly common (35% of stayers fall in this range), it stands out compared to the majority of stayers who have only 1-5 years of total experience. The model sees mid-level experience as a point where people often explore new horizons.

Third, working in the "other" sector (rather than medical or education) further contributed to the leave prediction. Only 22% of predicted stayers are in this category, suggesting that sector-specific stability or satisfaction patterns differ from yours.

Taken together, these elements outweighed positive signals like your medical insurance, recognition at work, and job stability. The organization should discuss your career goals and any external offers openly with you. You might consider what would make staying more attractive, such as clearer advancement paths or adjusted responsibilities, to reduce the risk of departure. (248 words)
